body: I know I have no veto powers here. I only recently became aware of the `if` part of the feature and think it's a mistake to merge this as is, as outlined here https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/82775#issuecomment-1919116854.
author: Voultapher

body:
We discussed this in today's @rust-lang/libs-api meeting. The consensus we came up with was:

We want to stabilize this. We're not thrilled with the module name `assert_matches` (`std::assert_matches::assert_matches!`), and would prefer a more general name there. However, we don't want to delay stabilization while trying to bikeshed that name. So, we're proposing that we leave the `assert_matches` *module* unstable for now (and let that bikeshed painting happen asynchronously), but go ahead and re-export the `assert_matches` macro from `std::prelude::rust_2024`, so that people can use it either by moving to Rust 2024 *or* by importing `std::prelude::rust_2024::assert_matches`.

Meanwhile, if someone comes up with a great idea for a module `assert_matches` should live in, we can move it there and stabilize that module.
author: joshtriplett

body: @joshtriplett to clarify, did the libs team talk about the concern I raised? Your comment does not mention it at all. That's why I'm asking.
author: Voultapher

body:
@Voultapher We did discuss your concern about the `if` syntax. Our conclusion is that it is more important for the syntax of `assert_matches` to be consistent with the one for `matches`.

If changes to the syntax are needed, this should be applied to both `matches` and `assert_matches`, although the bar for changing an already-stable API (`matches`) is very high. Regardless, this should be discussed separately from the stabilization of `assert_matches`.
author: Amanieu

body:
> Meanwhile, if someone comes up with a great idea for a module `assert_matches` should live in, we can move it there and stabilize that module.

Was a simple `core::assert` module considered? All of the assertion macros could live there, while still being re-exported from the root for compatibility. I know `core::assert::assert_matches!` is a bit of a stutter, but that's no different than `alloc::vec::Vec`, `core::sync::atomic::Atomic*`, etc.
author: cuviper

body: `core::assert` causes issues because importing will cause conflicts with the `assert` macro in the crate root.
author: Amanieu

body: Ah -- then maybe `core::assertions`, though that's a bit more of a mouthful. A broader `core::macros` wouldn't be horrible either IMO, but I could understand hesitation about that.
author: cuviper

body: @Amanieu thanks for clarifying and considering the point. While it's a bit unfortunate I don't see a better alternative either, that doesn't involve a time machine.
author: Voultapher

body:
> Ah -- then maybe `core::assertions`, though that's a bit more of a mouthful. A broader `core::macros` wouldn't be horrible either IMO, but I could understand hesitation about that.

We did consider `core::macros` as well. We're going to consider the module name further, but we wanted to let this proceed without waiting on the bikeshedding. :)

not following this pr too closely for now :bow: afaict there are some challenges in getting this to work correctly.

wanted to quickly chime in that i believe at some point https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/120222#issuecomment-1904152546 to be preferable simply because it's easier to confirm that it is actually correct.

> I believe this to be fairly straightforward by computing the vtable layout once for a fully generic princial, e.g. reusing the same vtable layout for all instances of `for<T, U> dyn Foo<T, U>`, regardless of the actual arguments.

for https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/120217 we could similarly simply forbid calling raw-ptr methods on trait objects/not making them object safe.

## Crater Report

### anymap 1.0

The most impactful regression is in [`anymap-1.0.0-beta.2`](https://crates.io/crates/anymap/1.0.0-beta.2) ([code](https://github.com/chris-morgan/anymap/blob/2e9a570491664eea18ad61d98aa1c557d5e23e67/src/any.rs#L37))
* cast kind: casting `dyn Trait` -> `dyn Trait + Auto` (adding autotraits)
* 65 dependents on anymap 1.0 in the crater report
* the code is copied to rust-analyzer/stdx ([code](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/26a16c4d9b081070a8b97c5437840e4e32ab3aa4/crates/stdx/src/anymap.rs#L284))
  * 23 additional dependents on RA/stdx (including other RA crates depending on stdx)
* anymap appears to be unmaintained ([advisory](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2021-0065.html)) and has multiple patched forks, including [`anymap3`](https://crates.io/crates/anymap3) and the one from RA above, getting this patched upstream seems unlikely

### other regressions

- [`serde_traitobject`](https://crates.io/crates/serde_traitobject) ([code](https://github.com/alecmocatta/serde_traitobject/blob/28eb9f2d52103be67913f52f755f5fe44b85d6ad/src/convenience.rs#L32))
  - cast kind: adding autotraits
  - 3 dependents in the crater report
  - The crate is using [nightly features](https://github.com/alecmocatta/serde_traitobject/blob/28eb9f2d52103be67913f52f755f5fe44b85d6ad/src/lib.rs#L103-L111), including `arbitrary_self_types`, so breaking it is probably fine.
- [`rsasl`](https://crates.io/crates/rsasl) ([code](https://github.com/dequbed/rsasl/blob/a8196a637ce40004cf44cd4c342127c8734aebe1/src/callback.rs#L296))
  - cast kind: casting `dyn Trait<'a>` to `dyn Trait<'b>`
  - 2 dependents in the crater report, both from [`vsmtp`](https://crates.io/crates/vsmtp), which appears to have gone closed source, but is still available on crates.io
- https://github.com/parperartifact/PPSMC crate `arun` ([code](https://github.com/parperartifact/PPSMC/blob/d44a07cb1e4ca10b304aca592529f06bf7ad55db/arun/src/lib.rs#L55))
  - cast kind: adding autotraits
  - no dependants
- [`gobject-subclass`](https://crates.io/crates/gobject-subclass) ([code](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gobject-subclass/blob/deb834bfa83e8e53b69024c4a5f7fadc3ac7489e/gobject-subclass/tests/simple_object.rs#L157))
  - cast kind: adding autotraits
  - cast is in a unit test
  - crate is deprecated
  - no dependants
- [`minfac`](https://crates.io/crates/minfac) ([code](https://github.com/mineichen/minfac/blob/3cd3becfe5f35d03513ef93cc249f274baaeb471/src/untyped.rs#L26))
  - cast kind: casting `dyn Fn(Foo)` ->  `dyn Fn()` ->  `dyn Fn(Foo)`
  - cast appears to be replaced with transmute on master branch
  - no dependants

body: For context, the alternative approach to fixing the soundness issues is by 1) making vtables less efficient by storing entries even if they should be unnecessary, preventing the casts from changing their layout this way and 2) restricting `#![feature(arbitrary_self_type)]` to not allow using method calls on raw pointers to trait objects.

body:
@rfcbot merge

We discussed this in the @rust-lang/lang meeting today and meeting consensus was to do the following:

* Approve breaking changes 1 (Generics must match) and 2 (Lifetimes must match).
* Approve breaking change 3 (Auto traits can't be added) but as a future-compatibility warning.

We are not opposed to a more precise check that would accept anymap but it in general would be better to just disallow this if we can. The anymap crate is a persistent problem because it hits the trifecta: leans on unsafe magic, unmaintained, and fills a real need and hence gets actual use. Rather than bending over backwards to accommodate it, we wanted to raise the possibility of taking it over somehow or issuing a new anymap crate, maybe adding it into the stdlib, *something* that will put us in a better position longer term.

body:
> This check makes the pointer metadata of a struct observable by `as` on stable rustc. Is this intended? So this means changing the ptr metadata of a struct in a library is a breaking change.

This behavior was not introduced by this PR, it's been like that [since Rust 1.2.0](https://rust.godbolt.org/z/fMxTYE5xb).

body: Don’t we have a way to conditionally compile code depending on whether system LLVM is used? I mildly remember us having to disable `fewer-names` unconditionally in that configuration because system-llvm was missing a patch that fixed quadratic inlining blowup with that option enabled. (Hence, probably, the `no-system-llvm` that stuck ever since in the relevant test)
author: nagisa

body:
> Don’t we have a way to conditionally compile code depending on whether system LLVM is used? I mildly remember us having to disable `fewer-names` unconditionally in that configuration because system-llvm was missing a patch that fixed quadratic inlining blowup with that option enabled. (Hence, probably, the `no-system-llvm` that stuck ever since in the relevant test)

If a test depends on a backported patch, you would use min-system-llvm-version in that case. Of course, this assumes that the patch is in the next upstream LLVM version, but we wouldn't accept the backport if that weren't the case.

body:
Visiting for weekly performance triage.

@DianQK the 1.8% regression to cargo opt-full is concerning to me. But from looking at the early rust-timer invocations, I saw it come up only once, not every time. So its not clear to me how much it was anticipated in your developments here.

Do you have any idea where the cargo opt-full regression is arising? Is it somehow connected to https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/78578 ?

(not marking as triaged, not yet.)
author: pnkfelix

body:
I don't think this is a regression. This is the result of previous try:  
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/120268#issuecomment-1985036234. I don't see cargo related regressions.
I made another attempt by revert this PR: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/122414. I can only see cranelift-codegen restoring the previous result.

Or maybe I'm missing something.
Usually, I think adding a fact may provide more opportunities for optimization. We need more work to optimize. This may be a desired result.

body:
I think we could check this directly in `push_suggestion`, so that no suggestions at all get reported on expansions of derives. Can you try that out and see if it works for you?

Adding a test for this is rather involved I'd presume, so manually testing it seems ok to me. But if you wanna try adding a test, we do have tests like [/home/ubuntu/rustc/rust10/tests/ui/proc-macro/derive-b.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/tests/ui/proc-macro/derive-b.rs) so you can probably just copy one of these tests and their derive and create a derive that will always emit your diagnostic.

body:
@oli-obk
Thank you for telling me. I checked the result of test and noticed that some valid suggestions are removed after modification.

```diff
--- a/tests/ui/pattern/usefulness/issue-119778-type-error-ice.stderr
+++ b/tests/ui/pattern/usefulness/issue-119778-type-error-ice.stderr
@@ -14,11 +14,6 @@ error[E0425]: cannot find value `S` in this scope
    |
 LL |     struct Foo([u8; S]);
    |                     ^ not found in this scope
-   |
-help: you might be missing a const parameter
-   |
-LL |     struct Foo<const S: /* Type */>([u8; S]);
-   |               +++++++++++++++++++++

 error[E0658]: `impl Trait` in type aliases is unstable
```

I think the reason of test failure is that the checks in `push_suggestion` are affecting other suggestions than casting (checking in `suggest_cast`). To minimize effect, I think it's better to check in `suggest_cast`.
I would like to hear your opinion.
author: long-long-float

body: I think it's ok to lose this suggestion if it is still reported in another error in the same test. If that is not the case, then we need to figure out why this code is marked as expanded by a derive.

I guess ideally we'd make the expansion somehow signal that it is referring to code copied from non-expanded code (in contrast to fully generated code, which is what the original issue was about).

That would require modifying our derives, and would not help for proc macro derives, for which I don't know how we can address it at this point.

body:
@oli-obk 
If the suggest position(Span) is within the original code's `derive(...)` in the original code, it can be suppressed. However it is possible that there is a correct suggestion even within the `derive(...)`.

I think the essence of this problem is that it is necessary to determine whether a suggestion is grammatically correct or not. It would be impossible to determine that using only `in_derive_expansion`. Even the simple method of judging in the first `suggest_cast` may suppress a correct suggestion.

As a different approach, I have an idea to check if the code to which the suggestion is applied is grammatically correct, and suppress it if it is not. I would like to implement a PoC if I can afford it.

body:
@oli-obk 
On second thought, your suggested method seems to solve the issue.
However, let me confirm that I did not fully understand how to implement it.

1. In derive exapantion, we store information about the derive's span in the expansion info `ExpnData` .
    
    ```rust
    // in ExpnData
    /// Whether this ExpnData is between an attribute `derive(...)`
    bool in_derive_attribute,
    ```
    
2. In `push_suggestion` , we check whether spans are in `derive(...)` using the information, not using `in_derive_expansion`
    - We just check `in_derive_attribute`
  
I don't (can't) take care about proc-macro now.

author: bjorn3

body:
I the long run it might be better to convert the `lib.rmeta` files to be valid Wasm object files.   This would match the ELF toolchain where `lib.rmeta` are valid ELF files.

Otherwise any user that sees the stderr of the linker (e.g. in the case of a link failure) will also see all these false-positive warnings on their screen (one per library).

Also, unlike ELF, the Wasm linker produces signature mismatch warnings, which is good to know about and the current setup (IIUC) now hides those because linker stderr is hidden by default.

body:
@rustbot labels -S-blocked -S-waiting-on-team

I'm going through things we've apparently been blocking awhile.  On this one, we had said:

> Our general sentiment was that things like this are why we do partial stabilizations, and that probably the harder bits of this shouldn't block the more straightforward bits of this from moving forward.

The original ask on the nomination was for us to agree to not do some parts of the original RFC.  That tends to be a hard ask of us (which means it can take a long time).  But you don't have to wait for us to agree that some parts of the RFC should never be done to land and propose stabilization on the parts that seem more obviously correct or well motivated.  As we mentioned, we're generally pretty happy to do partial stabilizations.

So I'm going to mark this as unblocked, because if this is implementing a part of an accepted RFC then it's OK to land in nightly as far as lang is concerned.

body: @scottmcm Do you consider the availability of the `const` `to_u8` and `to_char` methods blocking (and want them kept for now), or are you fine with this PR removing them for now?
author: joshtriplett

body:
@joshtriplett I think as long as there's *a* way to get the `u8` in `const`, I can tolerate it either way, and will leave it up to libs-api.  

(If that's `as u8` that's fine, but I wouldn't want to couple potential stabilization of this to needing stabilization of `impl const From`.  I also think that a method for getting the *specific* representation type is actually good, since to me the type might as well also be `i16: From<ascii::Char>` and such.)

body:
This change *as is* affects incremental compilation, making the change `fn foo<T>() {}` to `fn foo<T: Sized>() {}` now be picked up as a change. Haven't looked at the incr compilation machinery in a while, so I'm not sure how long it might take me to fix that.

Edit: figured out what the issue is. My change now only adds the implicit `Sized` obligation if there isn't an explicit one already. When testing incr comp, the first few cases use a flag to ignore spans, but because the predicate list doesn't change (there's always 1 Sized obligation, and it doesn't have `Span` state), adding an explicit `Sized` bound *doesn't* trigger a recompilation requirement (as long as spans are ignored).

Oof, Android libc actually segfaults the process when `abort()` is called. https://android.googlesource.com/platform/bionic/+/5f32207/libc/unistd/abort.c?pli=1#82

I guess then there are two options:

1. Treat SIGSEGV as a normal failure on Android
2. Continue printing "child process exited with signal 11" and disable the test on Android

I guess 1 is the least bad...
author: tmandry

author: tmandry

body:
> Oof, Android libc actually segfaults the process when `abort()` is called. https://android.googlesource.com/platform/bionic/+/5f32207/libc/unistd/abort.c?pli=1#82

That is an ancient version of bionic - the [current version](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/bionic/+/refs/heads/main/libc/bionic/abort.cpp#37) raises the signal, and if that doesn't work, eventually calls `exit`.

The [change](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/bionic/+/61e699a133a4807fe878a6cb0d7190d7c96e21f8) removing that intentional segfault is more than 10 years old, so that shouldn't be showing up in the test suite.

body:
> panic=immediate_abort 

I don't want to be a pedant, but there is no such thing unfortunately. The dead code elimination that `panic_immediate_abort` is supposed to induce requires re-optimizing the standard library (currently we require full recompilation but if we had mir-only rlibs I think it wouldn't), not just linking against a different panic runtime. I've thought about ways to make `panic=immediate_abort` work but so far all I've come up with is half measures or requires mir-only std. I'd be happy to discuss or work on improving this with anyone.

body:
> I was hoping that this PR would be sufficiently motivated by just the `cast_same_meta` example from the OP and "let's not break code that currently compiles", but evidently that's not the case, so here we are.

I agree that `cast_same_meta` should work, not sold on "let's not break code that currently compiles". I would expect that only using the adt tail for pointer casts won't break any actual code, even though it is theoretically breaking. I would very much prefer to try and break this for a "cleaner language" and only think about how to handle these overlapping impls if too many users are effected. We have `crater` for this.

I'd therefore be in favor of "Otherwise, I guess just normalizing to the metadata of the tail is an improvement over the status quo and all cases that it can break are easily fixed by adding `where Tail: Sized`."

author: lukas-code

body:
> I've updated the OP to show the differences between before and after this PR. I'm still not convinced that the "fallback impl" is better than a specialization, but I guess it doesn't matter too much. :shrug:

Neither am I. We already had that impl where we check for `Sized` for aliases and params. It is pretty much just an `AliasBound` candidate instead of an actual impl.

Pretty much what happens here is that if there's a `Sized` bound in the environment, either directly via `T: Sized` or indirectly from an item bound of `T: Trait` with `type Assoc: Sized`, we assume this means `Pointee<Metadata = ()>`. This is something the caller should prove. The only way you have an alias or an opaque as the self type (at least in the new solver) is if they are rigid as normalizing them relies on *the environment*.

We hackily reimplemented a super trait bound: `trait Sized: Pointee<Metadata = ()> {}`. I would like us to remove this manual builtin impl and instead add that super trait bound. That doesn't have to happen inside of this PR. I feel like we may have even considered to do so in the past but wasn't able to find anything skimming through previous PRs.

@lukas-code would you like to change it to a super trait right away or should we leave it to a future PR? If you want to not do so rn, please add a `FIXME` for it to the "fallback impl" arm in both solvers
author: lcnr

body: Making `Pointee<Metadata = ()>` a supertrait of `Sized` seems like a really good idea. I'll implement that and see what breaks 😆 .
author: lukas-code

body:
To answer the question of what breaks, it's this test: (in both solvers) https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4a2fe4491ea616983a0cf0cbbd145a39768f4e7a/tests/ui/sized/recursive-type-pass.rs#L1-L10

But that's probably fine, because that test compiling at all seems more like a side-effect of `Sized` being coinductive rather than intentional behavior. All other tests that rely on `Sized` being coinductive still pass.

But there are also a ton of [diagnostics regressions](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/fda5a39e060a1e5dea93542b91babf7f3512ac26), mostly complaining about "type mismatch resolving `<Foo as Pointee>::Metadata == ()`" in addition to "`Foo` is not sized". Fixing those seems to be non-trivial, so I'd like to move making `Pointee<Metadata = ()>` a supertrait of `Sized` to a future PR.

body:
> Can you explain what you mean? Not really sure what you're asking for.

There was discussion $somewhere recently that the `Output` type of `Fn` and `FnMut` should have been generic over the lifetime of the borrow of the closure context. If that was the case then I think we wouldn't need these AsyncFn traits?

I see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/119305 discusses this to some extent. I just wonder if we should track somewhere the idea of having LendingFn* eventually (or whether it is even possible to make the existing traits lending).

body:
These regressions are unsurprising, and I'd like to eventually re-support using async closures in `Fn`/`FnMut` when possible (exactly when there are no borrows from the closure type). Most of them aren't even ascribing the return type, which is one beneficial usage of async closures right now, so they can just write `async move ||` like `|| async move`.

This is ready for review.

body:
@cjgillot 

> I'm not convinced by the design chosen here. Codegen should not have to walk the MIR to check the presence of some instructions, that could easily degenerate into quadratic time-complexity. I'd rather see a re-design like the one started in #120193.

I'll give the redesign a try. So to sum up, it should:
- add the ExpectKind/cold_branches to mir switches
- update ast lowering to detect the intrinsics and generate the data

My concerns are:
- it'll probably add some complexity to opt passes in order to preserve the information
- can we make this work when the call to the intrinsics is inlined? I'd like to leave the door open for eventually exporting the intrinsics in std::hints

When I'm finished with it, should I open a new PR, or send you a link to the branch?

> Just like #120193 , every `SwitchInt` has `cold_targets` vector, which is used in the backend.

I already hinted in that PR how much of a footgun that extra vector may turn out to be. How can we limit this?
What about the alternate encoding I suggested?
author: cjgillot

body:
> I already hinted in that PR how much of a footgun that extra vector may turn out to be. How can we limit this? What about the alternate encoding I suggested?

If by footgun you mean updating optimization passes then it should not be necessary.

Basically with the redesign, there is a simple pass which fills in the `cold_targets` vectors and it's run _after_ optimization passes. When optimization passes run, all the `cold_targets` vectors are empty.

I will look into how the source scope data could be used. If it is something like metadata attached to MIR instructions, then my concern is that the information can be lost when optimization passes remove some instructions.

body: Note that LLVM recommends against emitting branch weights ourselves in https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/e3a470162738871bba982416748ae5f5e3572947. We should emit `expect` intrinsics as before.
author: Amanieu
x17jiri

body:
The reason the expect intrinsic isn't working is because we store its result to memory before reloading it in the unoptimized IR, which means it isn't recognized by LowerExpectIntrinsicPass:
```
  %4 = call i1 @llvm.expect.i1(i1 %0, i1 false)
  %5 = zext i1 %4 to i8
  store i8 %5, ptr %2, align 1
  %6 = load i8, ptr %2, align 1, !range !3, !noundef !4
  %7 = trunc i8 %6 to i1
  call void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(i64 1, ptr %2)
  br i1 %7, label %10, label %8
```

So this PR is still needed to ensure we emit suitable LLVM IR for LowerExpectIntrinsicPass.
author: Amanieu

body:
Rebased.

I noticed the intrisics were marked as stable. Note that for this fix to work, they can remain in the intrinsics module, but they cannot be real intrinsics. The implementation depends on `likely`/`unlikely` getting inlined so the compiler can see `cold_path`. And functions with `#[rustc_intrinsic]` are never inlined.
author: x17jiri

body:
Stealing review, I'm going to keep on top of this for the next few days to get it merged.
r? saethlin

> I noticed the intrisics were marked as stable.

I don't think they are, a little test program on a stable compiler refuses to compile because these are part of `core_intrinsics`.

> Note that for this fix to work, they can remain in the intrinsics module, but they cannot be real intrinsics.

Why can't they be real intrinsics? They're still unstable so we can reverse such changes, so I don't have a serious concern here.

I've tried this out locally and it looks good to me, so with my suggestions above squashed into the commit I'll approve.
author: saethlin

body:
> I don't think they are, a little test program on a stable compiler refuses to compile because these are part of `core_intrinsics`.

The attribute `rustc_const_stable_intrinsic` was added recently. I deleted it during rebase. I may have misunderstood what it means.

> Why can't they be real intrinsics? They're still unstable so we can reverse such changes, so I don't have a serious concern here.

They cannot have the `#[rustc_intrinsic]` attribute. The inline pass in Rust will never inline a function with this attribute. As I understand, this is because at the time the inline pass runs, it doesn't know if the backend will implement the intrinsic. But if they are not inlined and replaced with `cold_path`, they will not work
author: x17jiri

body:
> I noticed the intrisics were marked as stable.

What makes you think that?
If you are confused by rustc_const_stable_intrinsic, that just means that the intrinsic can be *indirectly* called by stable const code.

body: I *think* this fix will be nice to have in relnotes?
author: klensy

body: This is completely internal to the standard library implementation. Why would the relnotes mention it, and what would they say? We typically only document things that users need to be aware of. "Some functions are now hopefully a bit faster" doesn't go into relnotes.
author: RalfJung

body:
If the likely/unlikely intrinsics were broken before, and now they are fixed, then that information could be quite important to some users. Both to let them know that they can now again rely on these intrinsics doing something, and also to let them know that on previous versions of Rust it probably did nothing.

Assuming that this PR is about the unstable likely/unlikely intrinsics that are available to nightly users, and thus it's not completely internal to the standard library.
author: Kobzol

body: Relnotes generally don't mention changes to nightly features either. They document what changed with a *stable* release.
author: RalfJung

body: Someone used them to tune some perf and now they see that this *actually* only started working as expected, so less surprises.
author: klensy

body: Given that this is on nightly now, and relnotes will be put out in ~7 weeks, it also wouldn't make a lot of sense to attach this to the Rust 1.84 relnotes.
author: RalfJung

body: Right, I meant the [detailed release notes](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/releases/tag/1.82.0), which also mention internal changes and interesting pieces of information like this, not the main blog post.
author: Kobzol

body: How often do these detailed release notes talk about nightly features? In my understand, not very often. But maybe I misremember.
author: RalfJung

body: Personally, i think that release notes also should contain block for nightly changes, i.e. new added\removed unstable features to help users discover them, but this not related to current PR.
author: klensy

body: That would announce such changes on average 9 weeks too late. I don't think it makes a lot of sense.
author: RalfJung

body:
> That would announce such changes on average 9 weeks too late. I don't think it makes a lot of sense.

With release cycle of 6 weeks this will be only <= 6 weeks if placed in nearest relnotes.

How currently users can discover new features (before stabilization), excluding ones that manually track this repo? This gives lot less possible testing for that features. Or i miss something?
author: klensy

body:
Such updates can and often are posted to the tracking issues, and we expect interested users to follow those.

> With release cycle of 6 weeks this will be only <= 6 weeks if placed in nearest relnotes.

That would be really strange, since the codebase that is released there doesn't contain these changes.

If we want to do something like this IMO it should be a completely separate "nightly feature release notes" announcement, not part of the regular release notes. It doesn't even have to use the same 6 week cadence.

If we don't have good machine-applicable formatting then I'm opposed to this change because inserting text in a comment will trigger this and then require manually reflowing comment text.
author: the8472

body: (Nice, triaging age-old <kbd>needs-triage-legacy</kbd> issues and adding the relevant labels seems to have a positive effect ❤️)
author: fmease

body:
> If we don't have good machine-applicable formatting 

I don't think we will ever have that.

> then I'm opposed to this change because inserting text in a comment will trigger this and then require manually reflowing comment text.

That's the main purpose. If you add comments (or modify existing ones) and when the length exceeds the maximum size, tidy will give errors on those lines to enforce you to fix it. I believe this should be manageable, as there shouldn't be many errors in each pull request.
author: onur-ozkan

body:
> That's the main purpose. If you add comments (or modify existing ones) and when the length exceeds the maximum size, tidy will give errors on those lines to enforce you to fix it. 

Insert one word. Boom over the limit (which one might miss if one forgets to run tidy). PR fails. I need to go back and fix it and spill onto the next line. Which makes the next line-break awkward which means I have to reformat more lines....

I find this tiresome, unnecessary friction and of marginal benefit at best.

IMO linters should do one of these things:

* highlight real issues that require intervention
* automatically solve cosmetic issues
* get out of my way

Note that most comments already _aren't_ excessively long without the rule.
author: the8472

body:
I'm ok with tidy checking comment lengths (I thought it already did in fact, so I've been reflowing comments every time), but I'm not a fan of fixing everything automatically like this because it's not reliable enough.

If I were you I would put all of these 700 files to a list of exceptions in tidy, and either ignore them forever (not that bad), or ask people to go through them piece-by-piece. Unless you do intend to sort through all that by hand in which case I bow to you
author: Nadrieril

body: This affects over 6k lines which maybe suggests to me that people are comfortable with at least slightly longer lines for comments than this PR allows. Would it be worth experimenting with increasing the limit for comments, at least to start with?
author: ChrisDenton

body: I would agree with @bjorn3 here - people do a pretty good job of not adding very long comments as-is, I've not seen any significant PR discussion of "please reflow to fit X characters" (where a lint can help avoid review cycles), and it seems like comments are naturally a place where longer lengths may give more readability rather than less (e.g., diagrams, URLs, etc - I find limiting how these can be placed mostly unhelpful when I encounter it in other systems).

### Summary

In conclusion, this crater run revealed that making the lint deny-by-default (which is NOT the default that would would be used, it would be warn-by-default) could break 7057 crates / 851203 crates tested (0.82%), there was a total of 116165 errors, of which 107531 (92.6%) errors were coming from derive macros, 2150 were coming from `macro_rules!` and 6484 errors are not coming from either of them.

Analysing the root of those derives and macros revealed many outdated versions of `serde_derive` and `diesel_derives`, representing nearly 74% of the total errors alone, as well ~~6~~ 4 different derive crates that represent 11.4% that would need to be updated.

To put it simply:

 - 91711 (82.8%) errors would be fixed by `cargo update` (representing 6104 different crates)
 - 5472 (4.9%) errors that could fixed by upstream change (at least ~~6~~ 4 different derive crates)
 - 6484 (5.9%) errors requires manual intervention (788 different crates)
 - 7309 (6.6%) uncategorised errors (probably manual intervention and deps change): 

I think those are more than acceptable numbers, in more that 4/5 of cases a `cargo update` would fix the warnings and by fixing ~~6~~ 4 different derives we could get closer to 90%, the rest of cases would need manual interventions, but some interventions are to be expected.

*Reminder that the lint is warn-by-default, so it wouldn't actually break any crates!*

*Btw, I created a python script [`report.py`](https://gist.github.com/Urgau/edc4f767025d608776ed5fa8446f138b), just for this. :-)*

body:
@rylev I tried very hard in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/121625 to fix the perf regression, but it when mostly nowhere. My latest (and most promising) attempt end up having a correctness issue.

At some point I was wondering why diesel was the only benchmark to show any regressions (even in incremental), just to realize that in the Crater run some older versions of the crate were affect by the lint; and indeed it now produces 155 warnings!

No wonder why my all attempts went no-where.

_If only I could have gotten kcachegrind working earlier it would have screamed this to me; it shows that 99.39% the instructions in the lint is the diagnostic machinery._

So in summary, there is no perf-regression per se, `rustc` is now _just_ doing way more work because it has to display more than 155 different warnings.

body:
Note that some standard keyboard layouts have a key combo (often altgr+m) that produces the `U+00B5 μ
MICRO SIGN` output, so this is easier to type. We also don't use `U+2212 − MINUS SIGN` for operators.
author: the8472

body:
> suggested that the old byte sequence is a lot more compatible than the new one

Yeah so it was added in the era Unicode was trying hard for 1:1 mappings with other encodings. Quite often these encodings were 8-bit encodings using the upper "unused" half of ASCII, and Unicode often encoded these characters with the same lower byte as their original encoding.

In particular, this comes from Latin-1 and Windows-1252: In U+00B5 MICRO SIGN, in UTF8, will render as Âµ (since it's `C2 B5`). These encodings also happen to be the most common way for a system to be configured when it's not configured for Unicode.

Unicode is actually at this moment working on publishing data for "do not emit" code points and sequences, which lists code points and sequences that should be recognized by software but not produced. The draft is [here](https://www.unicode.org/L2/L2024/24021-do-not-emit.txt), it doesn't currently include the micro sign but that could be an oversight since it does include other deprecated characters. It was compiled from various scattered unicode sources and it's likely that [UAX 25](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr25/) was not one of them. I brought it up with the author of that file.

-----

I'm ambivalent here: I think ideally we should not produce legacy characters, but "wanting better compat with legacy encodings" is exactly why these exist (and aren't marked as being banned entirely), and from that other thread this is clearly something people care about.

So it's a matter of how much "we should not produce legacy characters" weighs up against "we want stuff to still work okayishly well on misconfigured terminals". And also whether `Âµ` counts as "okayishly well".


Personally I'm not a huge fan of trying hard to appease misconfigurations but at the same time I have often been frustrated with how hard it is to correctly configure stuff, especially when there are multiple steps in the pipeline that need configuring. I've mentioned this before in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75065, but "i am using `screen` over `ssh` over my local terminal emulator" is a situation i've been in often where figuring out what needs to be configured correctly can take a lot of time.


So, anyway, with my unicode expert hat on, I think there are arguments for going both ways, it's up to the relevant team to weigh them.
author: Manishearth

body:
I checked, UAX 25 is not a normative standard, and it's largely focused on the context of mathematical stuff only.

I would say that overall while UAX 25 does consider it a legacy character in the scope of stuff it is talking about, Unicode does not consider it a legacy character _overall_. I think it's fine to use the greek letter for micro, but it's also fine to use the micro sign.


It is unlikely the micro sign will make it into the DoNotEmit file I mentioned earlier.
author: Manishearth

body:
@Jules-Bertholet What is the motivation for this change? Did you run into any situation where U+00B5 didn't work as well as U+03BC?

(As far as I know, U+00B5 works in more situations than U+03BC, which is why I think we should prefer U+00B5.)
author: m-ou-se

body:
> What is the motivation for this change?

Just trying to follow UTR 25's recommendation.
author: Jules-Bertholet

body:
> Just trying to follow UTR 25's recommendation.

In that case, I'm going to close this, since there are concrete downsides to using U+03BC. Feel free to re-open if you think Rust users experience any practical downsides from using U+00B5.

> there's a trivial change to the license list and I'm not sure I'm supposed to self-approve that.

There's nobody assigned to the PR (since you requested a "ghost" review) so nobody else will look at it either.

In this case, given that this is already a rustc dependency, this seems fine.

> These syncs are pretty painful when the repositories drift apart.

FWIW, in my experience doing these syncs for Miri, it helps a lot to automate as much as possible and do them more often. We have a script that creates the PR fully automatically (for Miri -> rustc syncs); I run that almost every weekend and it is usually entirely pain-free. For the other direction we have a CI cronjob that creates a PR automatically whenever Miri no longer builds against rustc master.

> There's nobody assigned to the PR (since you requested a "ghost" review) so nobody else will look at it either.

Oh, I thought the CCed people would look at it.

> FWIW, in my experience doing these syncs for Miri, it helps a lot to automate as much as possible and do them more often.

We do it every week(-ish) as well, but recently ran into a lot of bootstrap and lint related issues, like the "unknown `cfg`" lint, and stuff related to linking to `rustc_driver`; some of them wouldn't even show up on the PR CI, just on bors.

The other thing is that `git subtree` seems to report more conflicts than expected, even ones I've fixed before. There was one that showed up on every sync for I don't know, 6 months or maybe a year. It was auto-fixable, fortunately, and I think it went away recently when Veykril removed the code.

We were also stopping merges on the rust-analyzer side until the sync back (rust -> rust-analyzer), because if the rust-analyzer repository changed, we'd get more conflicts. What helped here was doing the sync back only up to the release commit, not up to master. So instead of:

1. merge rust-analyzer release into rustc master
2. fetch rustc master
3. subtree rustc master into a rust-analyzer branch
4. merge rust-analyzer master into the new branch
5. merge the new branch into rust-analyzer

This works much better:

1. merge rust-analyzer release into rustc master
2. fetch rustc master
3. subtree rustc master into a rust-analyzer branch
4. merge rust-analyzer release into the new branch
5. merge rust-analyzer master into the new branch
6. merge the new branch into rust-analyzer

> For the other direction we have a CI cronjob that creates a PR automatically whenever Miri no longer builds against rustc master.

We always sync both ways, not only when it stops building, because of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/pull/13676.

I think you're using `josh` now, maybe that one is more resilient, I haven't tried it yet.
author: lnicola

body:
Ouch. :( Okay that sounds quite painful. Not sure why it's so much worse for RA than for Miri. Do you have a lot of conflicts? We do syncs in the two directions largely independent of each other and that works fine; that seems to be a subtree vs josh-proxy issue. But if the "sync both ways" can be automated that should not in itself be such a big deal I would expect. But maybe I am underestimating this, having to coordinate multiple branches does sound like significant overhead.

The git master version of josh is pretty reliable, yeah. (The latest released version still has an issue that can sometimes be blocking.) Happy to talk more if you want to explore switching RA to josh (but probably best to start a new thread e.g. on Zulip of that rather than discussing it here).
author: RalfJung

body:
> Do you have a lot of conflicts?

We used to freeze `master` during the syncs, but that wasn't strictly enforced and some of them took 2-3 days because of other PRs in the queue (that is, ignoring the CI/bors failures). So not a lot of conflicts in practice, but before my two-step merge trick, every "real" conflict would show up again on every further change to the same file up to `master`.

body:
Hm, the move to `NtWriteFile` was done for soundness reasons, with the intent to keep open the option of moving back (or to another function) should that become viable.

That said, I'm pretty sure `WriteFile` behaves the same way as `NtWriteFile` considering the former wraps the latter. And tbh I don't think it can work any other way than zeroing the bytes. The docs for [`SetFileValidData`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-setfilevaliddata) have a long discussion on the security implications of uninitialized file data. And the whole reason that function exists as a separate thing is to silo such concerns (and the privileges it requires). My complete guess is that the microsoft docs are hedging based on old (win95?) behaviour.

Which is a long winded way of saying I'll probably accept this but I'd want to check in with a few people first.
author: ChrisDenton
